lead: A pretrained language model is a Transformer that has already learned language from a large pile of unlabelled text, so you can reuse its weights on your own small labelled dataset. Labelling ten thousand sentences by hand can cost lakhs; raw text is free. BERT reads a sentence in both directions and fills in blanks. GPT reads left to right and predicts the next token. Both sit inside modern search, tagging, translation and chatbots.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for the Transformer block, Unit 4 for language modelling and word embeddings, and Unit 1 for cross-entropy.

blocks.text: A supervised model needs a label for every input. Text already carries its own label: hide part of a sentence and ask the model to recover it. This is self-supervised learning, and it is the whole reason pretraining exists — billions of web pages can be used without paying a single annotator.
The result is a set of weights that encodes general language: grammar, word senses, common facts. You then reuse it in one of two ways.

items: Fine-tuning: add a small task head and update every weight on your labelled data. A few thousand examples are often enough.
Feature extraction: freeze the pretrained weights and train only the head. Cheaper, usually a little weaker, and the right choice when your dataset is tiny.

blocks.text: The fine-tuning recipe is three steps.

items: Load the pretrained checkpoint and attach a task head.
Train with a small learning rate, roughly 2e-5 to 5e-5, for three or four epochs.
Evaluate on the task benchmark, for example the GLUE suite of sentence-level tasks (acceptability, sentiment, inference, paraphrase, similarity).

blocks.text: BERT means Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. It is an encoder-only stack, built as in 5.2 but with no causal mask, so every position sees both its left and right context at the same time.

items: Pick 15% of the tokens at random.
Replace 80% of those with [MASK], 10% with a random vocabulary token, and leave 10% unchanged.
Predict the original token at every chosen position with a softmax over the vocabulary.
Compute cross-entropy only at the chosen positions; the untouched 85% adds nothing to the loss.

blocks.where: M is the set of chosen positions, xᵢ is the true token there, x̃ is the corrupted sentence, and p is the model's softmax probability for that token.

blocks.text: The 80/10/10 split matters. If every chosen token became [MASK], the model would never see the symbol [MASK] during fine-tuning, and the random 10% forces it to distrust the input token rather than copy it. Two special tokens complete the input: [CLS] sits first and its final state is the whole-sentence vector used for classification, while [SEP] marks where one segment ends and the next begins. The original paper also trained next sentence prediction, asking whether segment B follows A; later work showed it adds little, and RoBERTa dropped it.
BERT-base has 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 heads and about 110 million parameters. BERT-large has 24 layers, 1024 hidden, 16 heads and about 340 million.

sections.h3: GPT, the other families, and metrics

blocks.text: GPT is decoder-only. A causal mask lets position i attend only to positions up to i, so the model computes p(token t+1 | tokens 1…t) and nothing more. Every token in the corpus is therefore a training example, far denser than BERT's 15%. The family grew fast: GPT-1 had about 117 million parameters, GPT-2 about 1.5 billion, GPT-3 about 175 billion. Scaling that run is 5.4.

blocks.where: L is the mean cross-entropy loss in nats per token, so perplexity is the number of equally likely tokens the model is effectively choosing among. Lower is better; 1 would be perfect certainty. If your loss is in bits, use PPL = 2^L instead; both forms give the same number.

blocks.text: Encoder-decoder models such as T5 and BART use both halves: an encoder reads the input bidirectionally and a decoder writes the output left to right. They suit translation and summarisation, where input and output are different sequences. NVIDIA NeMo is a toolkit for building and fine-tuning these models — it is not a model family.

Where you attach the task head depends on the family. For a classifier on an encoder, attach a head to the [CLS] state; on a decoder-only model, attach it to the state at the final position. For tagging or question answering, attach heads to the token states. Fine-tuning updates all weights; prompting changes none of them and belongs to 5.6.

figure.caption: Unlabelled text feeds two objectives: masking for BERT's encoder and next-token prediction for GPT's decoder. Notice that both stacks end at the same reuse step, fine-tuning or prompting.

spec.title: Two pretraining objectives
spec.aria: Unlabelled text feeds two branches, masked language modelling into an encoder stack for BERT and next-token prediction into a decoder stack for GPT, and both branches end at fine-tune or prompt.

examples.question: (a) A BERT masked-LM head reads 'the cat sat on the [MASK]'. It gives P(mat) = 0.5, P(floor) = 0.2, P(dog) = 0.1, and 0.2 spread over all remaining words. Find the cross-entropy loss at this position in nats and in bits. (b) A small GPT scores the three true tokens of a sequence with probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125. Find its perplexity on that sequence.
steps: (a) The true token is mat, predicted with probability 0.5.
Perplexity = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.0, so the model is as unsure as choosing among 4 equally likely tokens.
examples.answer: The masked-LM loss is 0.6931 nats, which is 1.0 bit; the GPT's perplexity is 4.0.
examples.check:
import math
p = 0.5
loss = -math.log(p)
print(round(loss, 3))
print(round(loss / math.log(2), 3))
probs = [0.5, 0.25, 0.125]
prod = 1.0
for q in probs:
    prod *= q
print(round(prod ** (-1 / 3), 3))

traps: BERT cannot generate text: its masked objective needs the whole sentence at once, so there is no left-to-right order to sample from.
15% is the fraction of tokens chosen, and only 80% of those become [MASK], so the real mask rate is 12% of all tokens.
Few-shot examples in a prompt change no weights. Prompting is inference; only gradient steps update parameters.

Perplexity must match the log base of the loss: PPL = exp(L) when L is in nats, and PPL = 2^L when L is in bits. The two give the same number. Mixing them — exp of a bit-loss, or 2^L of a nat-loss — gives a wrong value.
NVIDIA NeMo is a toolkit for building and fine-tuning models, not a model family like BERT or GPT.

quiz.q: State the pretraining objective of BERT and of GPT in one line each.
quiz.a: BERT: predict randomly masked tokens from both-side context (masked language modelling). GPT: predict the next token from the left context only (autoregressive language modelling).

quiz.q: Give the layer count, hidden size, head count and parameter count of BERT-base and BERT-large.
quiz.a: BERT-base: 12 layers, hidden 768, 12 heads, about 110M parameters. BERT-large: 24 layers, hidden 1024, 16 heads, about 340M parameters.

quiz.q: Why does BERT replace only 80% of chosen tokens with [MASK] instead of all of them?
quiz.a: Because [MASK] never appears at fine-tuning time, a model trained only on [MASK] would face a distribution it has never seen. Mixing in random and unchanged tokens forces it to build a real representation of every input token.

quiz.q: Contrast fine-tuning with feature extraction for a pretrained encoder.
quiz.a: Fine-tuning updates all pretrained weights plus a new head, so it needs more compute and more labelled data but gives the best accuracy. Feature extraction freezes the encoder and trains only the head; it is cheaper and safer on tiny datasets.

quiz.q: A masked-LM head gives P(a) = 0.4 for the correct token and spreads 0.6 over the rest. Compute the loss in nats and in bits.
A GPT assigns the true tokens of a 2-token sequence probabilities 0.8 and 0.5. Compute the perplexity.
A team wants a model to write product descriptions from a short spec. Explain why they should not pick a BERT encoder for the writing step itself.
quiz.a: BERT is trained to fill blanks with the full sentence visible, so its representations of later positions already contain the words it would have to produce. Generation needs p(next token | prefix) computed without seeing the future. A causal decoder, that is a GPT-style model or the decoder half of T5/BART, is the correct choice; BERT can still help by encoding the spec and tagging the output.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry most teams never pretrain from scratch: they start from an open checkpoint and fine-tune or prompt it. Domain pretraining on a hospital's own notes or a bank's own circulars still pays off when the vocabulary is unusual. Encoder models remain the cheap option for search and tagging, since a 110-million-parameter encoder runs on a CPU. Sentence-embedding models built from BERT power the vector search behind many product catalogues. Search next for RoBERTa, DeBERTa, sentence-transformers and IndicBERT.
